title: Forest-Based Graph Learning for Semi-Supervised Node Classification
claim: Prior paradigms aggregate messages over dense graph edges; ours routes global messages along sparse spanning trees.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, same graph with highlighted edges in right panel
description: Two side-by-side panels show the same small graph of gray circular nodes joined by edges, with one red target node labeled u in the middle. In the left panel all edges are thin gray lines, and dashed red arrows flow along nearly every edge toward u. This shows dense, local message passing. In the right panel the same graph is drawn again, but a subset of edges forming a spanning tree is thick and black. Dashed red arrows flow only along the tree edges, from leaves toward u, and the remaining edges stay thin gray. The red node and red arrows draw the eye first. The contrast between thin and thick edges shows that the sparse tree structure carries the aggregation. There is no text apart from u.
caption: Our paradigm (right) utilizes the most sparse structures of a graph, i.e., spanning trees, to aggregate global messages against the prior paradigms (left).
abstract: Existing Graph Neural Networks usually learn long-distance knowledge via stacked layers or global attention, but struggle to balance cost-effectiveness and global receptive field. In this work, we break the dilemma by proposing a novel forest-based graph learning (FGL) paradigm that enables efficient long-range information propagation. Our key insight is to reinterpret message passing on a graph as transportation over spanning trees that naturally facilitates long-range knowledge aggregation, where several trees--a forest--can capture complementary topological pathways. Theoretically, we demonstrate that as edge-homophily estimates improve, the induced distribution biases towards higher-homophily trees, which enables generating a high-quality forest by refining a homophily estimator. Furthermore, we propose a linear-time tree aggregator that realizes quadratic node-pair interactions. Empirically, our framework achieves comparable results against state-of-the-art counterparts on semi-supervised node classification tasks while remaining efficient. Codes are available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FGL/}.
